extra.message: Password reset token returned to requester enables full account takeover — Any attacker who knows a victim's email address can take over that account (buyer, vendor_manager, admin, or support_agent) without any access to the victim's inbox. [verified: password_reset_request returns mock_reset_token in the HTTP response for any submitted email and stores it as the valid reset_token_hash; anyone can then call password-reset/confirm with that token to fully take over the account without email access.]

Server-side template injection via string-built Jinja2 template — Remote code execution via classic Jinja2 SSTI sandbox-escape payloads. [verified: fragment is concatenated into the Jinja2 template source itself before compilation, enabling classic SSTI/RCE payloads; no sanitization is applied.]

OS command injection via unsanitized host parameter — Full remote code execution on the application server. [verified: host is concatenated directly into os.system with no shell-escaping or allowlisting; the only guard is a shared internal token header, not input validation.]

Password reset token disclosed directly in client UI — Full account takeover for any user whose email is known/guessed, plus account enumeration, without needing access to the victim's email inbox. [verified: password_reset_request (main.py:701-710) always returns mock_reset_token in the response body when a matching non-disabled user exists, with no email delivery or auth check, and the frontend just prints it — anyone who knows a victim's email can fetch the real reset token and take over the account.]

Hardcoded/default APP_SECRET_KEY fallback — An attacker who knows the default secret can forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, or password-reset tokens for any account, achieving full account takeover including admin [verified: secret_key falls back to a hardcoded literal with no startup check rejecting it in production, and this key signs session/CSRF/reset tokens, enabling forgery if defaults are kept.]

Path traversal / arbitrary file write via unsanitized filename parameters — Arbitrary file write outside the intended export directory, potentially overwriting application code or planting a web shell. [verified: packet_ref/name are joined directly into a filesystem path with no traversal stripping (unlike the main app's safe_filename pattern), allowing writes outside the export dir.]

Reflected/stored XSS via unescaped |safe render of user input — Script execution in the context of the application origin (session/token theft, UI redress) for anyone who views the crafted URL/response. [verified: card is rendered via {{ card|safe }} which explicitly disables autoescaping on attacker-controlled input, returned as HTML — classic reflected XSS.]

XXE via DTD/external-entity resolution enabled on user-supplied XML — Arbitrary local file read (e.g. secrets, source code) and SSRF against internal services. [verified: XMLParser is configured with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False on raw attacker-supplied body, enabling file disclosure and SSRF via external entities.]

Insecure cookie Secure flag defaults to false — Session and CSRF cookies transmitted over unencrypted HTTP can be intercepted by a network attacker, leading to session hijacking and CSRF bypass [verified: cookie_secure defaults to false unless explicitly overridden, and is used directly for session/CSRF cookie flags, allowing cleartext transmission on default/misconfigured deployments.]

CSV formula injection in admin/vendor exports — Formula/DDE execution in the spreadsheet application of an admin or vendor opening an exported CSV, potentially leading to local code execution or data exfiltration via remote formulas [verified: Same csv_response sink at main.py:1846-1860 is reused by both admin and vendor export endpoints without any escaping of formula-trigger characters, so the injected values execute when opened in spreadsheet software.]

Open redirect via unvalidated redirect target — Phishing / credential-harvesting via a trusted-looking redirect origin. [verified: lane is passed unchecked into RedirectResponse with no same-origin/allowlist validation, enabling arbitrary open redirects.]

Mass assignment via unrestricted dict.update from request body — Attacker can set arbitrary/sensitive fields (approval flags, balances, roles) directly from client input. [verified: workset.update(payload) merges raw request JSON over a trusted default dict with no allow-list, letting a caller set approved/balance/role fields.]

Secret Authorization header written to application logs — Any party with log access (or a log-aggregation leak) can recover bearer tokens/API keys and impersonate the caller. [verified: the raw Authorization header value is written verbatim to logs via logger.warning, persisting bearer credentials in plaintext logs.]

Reflected CORS origin with credentials enabled — Any malicious website can make authenticated cross-origin requests to this endpoint (and, if credentials/session cookies are involved elsewhere, exfiltrate sensitive data) on behalf of a logged-in victim. [verified: Origin header is reflected verbatim into Access-Control-Allow-Origin alongside Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, the canonical misconfiguration allowing any origin credentialed access.]

NoSQL injection via unvalidated MongoDB filter — Unauthorized data disclosure or query-logic bypass against the backing Mongo store. [verified: the full attacker-controlled JSON is passed unvalidated as a MongoDB filter to find_one, permitting operator injection to bypass query logic.]
